summary: A 1971 note by P. M. Karp about a network meeting. It was updated by RFC 116.
questions: where was the may 1971 network working group meeting
who organized hotel reservations for the nwg meeting
subtitle: A short 1971 notice about where the Network Working Group would meet next, and how to book rooms.

tldr.problem: The Network Working Group needed to tell its members where and when its next meeting would be held.
tldr.mechanism: The note gives the place (Atlantic City, New Jersey, alongside the SJCC), the reserved room and dates, and says reservations will be handled through MITRE so attendees stay at the same hotel.
tldr.outcome: It is a logistics notice, not a protocol. The unit metadata shows it was updated by RFC 116.

today: RFC 99 is a meeting notice with no listed obsoleting document; it was updated by RFC 116.

sections.title: The Meeting Announcement
sections.content: RFC 99 announces that the next meeting of the Network Working Group will be held in Atlantic City, New Jersey, at the same time as the SJCC. The Wicker Room of the Dennis Hotel has been reserved from Sunday, May 16 at 8:00 pm through Thursday, May 20 at 6:00 pm.
sections.plainLanguage: It says where the club will meet and for how many days the room is saved for them.

sections.title: Booking Rooms Through MITRE
sections.content:
It was not possible to reserve a block of hotel rooms. The author therefore proposes to try to place all attendees at the same hotel by handling reservations through MITRE.

Prospective attendees are asked to contact the author's secretary, Mrs. Marybelle Goodson, by telephone.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the hotel would not save a bunch of beds, one office will collect everyone's requests so the whole group sleeps in the same place.

sections.title: Where It Fits
sections.content: The RFC is a one-page note by P. Karp of MITRE, dated 22 February 1971. It defines no protocol and has no technical content. The unit metadata records that RFC 116 updates it.
sections.plainLanguage: It is just a friendly notice, not a set of rules for computers.
